title: Coniglio alla cacciatora
subtitle: Hunter's-style braised rabbit with tomato, wine, and herbs
excerpt: Coniglio alla cacciatora is the hunter's rabbit: pieces of rabbit braised in white wine, tomato, garlic, rosemary, and sage. The same cacciatora method applies to chicken, but rabbit absorbs the herb braise more deeply and repays the longer cooking time. This is central Italian autumn cooking at its most direct.
sourceNotes: Central Italian regional recipe. Hunter's-style rabbit appears across Tuscany, Umbria, and the Marche, wherever rabbit is hunted. Method drawn from Pellegrino Artusi, La scienza in cucina e l'arte di mangiar bene (1891, public domain), and traditional cacciatora preparations.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Better made a day ahead. Reheat very gently.

glossaryTerms.definition: Italian for 'in the hunter's style'; dishes alla cacciatora are braised in wine, tomato, and herbs, using the vegetables and aromatics a hunter might carry into the field.

content.text: is rabbit browned and then braised in white wine, tomato, garlic, and herbs. It follows the same logic as chicken cacciatora but the rabbit needs a little longer in the pot: about an hour from start to finish. The meat should be tender and pulling easily from the bone.
Season {{rabbit}} of rabbit pieces, dust in {{plain-flour}} of flour. Heat {{olive-oil}} of olive oil in a casserole and brown the pieces in batches over high heat, 4 minutes per side. Remove.

Add {{garlic}} of garlic, rosemary, and sage to the pan. Cook 1 minute. Pour in {{dry-white-wine}} of wine, scraping up the pan. Reduce by half. Add {{tinned-tomatoes}} of crushed tomatoes. Return the rabbit. Cover and braise over medium-low heat for 50 minutes, turning once, until the meat pulls from the bone.
Uncover for the final 10 minutes to thicken the sauce. Season and serve with polenta or bread.

items.cause: Cooked at too high a temperature.
items.fix: Rabbit is lean and dries out quickly at high heat. Keep the braise at a very gentle simmer, covered.

content.text: Cacciatora preparations are found across Tuscany, Umbria, the Marche, and Lazio, wherever rabbit is hunted. Rabbit is the traditional choice; chicken cacciatora is the everyday home version. The braise uses wine, tomatoes, and herbs: everything a hunter might carry into the field.
